label: Exercises for Prologue and Act I
notes: This review deck spans printed pages twenty-four through twenty-eight. We turn the Prologue and Act I into a problem-solving lab, revisiting ultimate equality, angular excess, the sign of Gaussian curvature, and non-Euclidean geometry by working representative problems rather than restating the text.

label: Three Results to Carry Forward
notes: Before solving anything we pin down the three load-bearing results from Act I. Ultimate equality justifies the derivative, angular excess measures intrinsic bending, and the sign of curvature sorts surfaces into sphere-like, flat, and saddle-like. Every exercise that follows leans on exactly one of these.

label: Warm-Up: Ultimate Equality for the Cube
notes: We start with Newton's ultimate-equality idea applied to the cube. The secant ratio is a finite chord that we shrink until the discarded terms vanish in the limit. Keeping the bookkeeping visible shows precisely which pieces survive and why the answer equals three x squared.

label: Angular Excess, Made Precise
notes: Here we make angular excess precise. A geodesic triangle has interior angles whose sum exceeds pi on a positively curved surface. The excess is the deviation from the flat sum, and the local Gauss-Bonnet statement equates it to the total curvature captured inside the triangle's boundary.

label: Worked Problem: The Spherical Octant
notes: Our flagship computation is the triple-right-angled triangle on a sphere. Three mutually perpendicular great-circle arcs bound one octant. Each corner is a right angle, so the angle sum is three halves pi and the excess is exactly pi over two, matching one eighth of the total sphere.

label: Excess Equals Area Times Curvature
notes: We generalize the octant result to any spherical triangle. The excess equals the enclosed area divided by the radius squared, which is the area times the constant curvature. Checking the octant against this formula confirms the bookkeeping and ties angle defect directly to measurable area.

label: Sorting Surfaces by Curvature Sign
notes: Next we sort three model surfaces by curvature sign. The sphere closes triangles with positive excess, the plane and the rolled cylinder keep angle sums at pi, and the saddle spreads triangles into angle deficit. Sign, not magnitude, decides which non-Euclidean world we inhabit.

label: Worked Problem: The Cylinder Is Intrinsically Flat
notes: This exercise confronts the common error that a cylinder is curved. Intrinsically it is flat: unrolling it onto paper preserves every distance and angle, so its Gaussian curvature is zero. The lesson is that bending in space is extrinsic and invisible to a surface dweller measuring triangles.

label: Worked Problem: Pythagorean Triples on the Circle
notes: We revisit Euclidean geometry through Pythagoras. Sweeping a line of rational slope from a fixed point on the unit circle produces a second rational point, and clearing denominators yields a Pythagorean triple. This makes the algebra of right triangles a geometric construction the reader can rerun.

label: Measuring Curvature From the Inside
notes: Now we invert the excess law to measure curvature intrinsically. Lay down a small geodesic triangle, sum its angles, subtract pi, and divide by the area. As the triangle shrinks the ratio converges to the Gaussian curvature at the point, needing no embedding in space.

label: Worked Problem: A Tessellation Excess Ledger
notes: We scale up to a tessellation, summing the excess of every spherical face. Each face contributes its own angle defect, and the column total recovers four pi, the integral of curvature over the whole sphere. This is Gauss-Bonnet appearing as a simple additive ledger.

label: The Lab Protocol and What Survives
notes: We close with the construct, measure, compare, perturb protocol that turns each exercise into a reproducible lab. Build a model, measure an invariant, compare it with a theorem, then change one parameter and watch what survives. The surviving quantity is the geometry the chapter teaches.
